1.pericope_label: But Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished all his house.

schools.summary: Gill sets the thirteen years against the seven the sanctuary had taken and reads the difference as deliberate: Solomon made more haste with the house of God than with his own, showing greater regard to God's honour than to his own glory or convenience, and did not begin the palace until the temple was finished.
Clarke is concerned with the site, placing the house in Jerusalem as the king's probable winter residence and noting that a later chapter calls it simply the king's house.

Henry turns the comparison into a principle — the king built for God first and all his other building was comfortable after it; he was not more exact on his own house but less eager, in no haste for a palace while the sanctuary was unfinished — and refuses to make the verse a reproach against David, since a son may build better than his father in proportion to the estate God gave him.

themes: But Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished all his house.

2.pericope_label: He built also the house of the forest of Lebanon; the length thereof was an hundred cubits, and the breadth thereof fifty cubits, and the height thereof thirty cubits, upon four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams upon the pillars. And it was covered with cedar above upon the beams, that lay on forty five pillars, fifteen in a row. And there were windows in three rows, and light was against light in three ranks. And all the doors and posts were square, with the windows: and light was against light in three ranks.

schools.summary: Delitzsch derives the name from the architecture — a house built of a forest of cedar pillars — records the Arabic house of his arms without reducing it to an arsenal, and argues that the forty-five and the fifteen belong to the side-chambers rather than the pillars, giving three tiers of fifteen rooms each; on the doorways he prefers to read the word square of the openings rather than their frames.

Gill denies the house stood on Lebanon, which lay far to the north while this building served as both an armoury and a court, and derives the name from its cedar and its setting among resembling groves; he takes it for a summer house, cites the Targum's royal house of refreshment, and distributes the forty-five pillars in three rows of fifteen across the second floor.
Clarke agrees it was not built in Lebanon, places it on Mount Zion, and can only guess that the name followed the materials brought from there.

debates.question: What do the forty-five, fifteen to a row, count?

positions.position: Pillars, set in three rows of fifteen on the second floor.
Side-chambers built upon the lower rows of pillars, in three tiers of fifteen.

themes: He built also the house of the forest of Lebanon; the length thereof was an hundred cubits, and the breadth thereof fifty cubits, and the height thereof thirty cubits, upon four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams upon the pillars.
And it was covered with cedar above upon the beams, that lay on forty five pillars, fifteen in a row.
And there were windows in three rows, and light was against light in three ranks.
And all the doors and posts were square, with the windows: and light was against light in three ranks.

6.pericope_label: And he made a porch of pillars; the length thereof was fifty cubits, and the breadth thereof thirty cubits: and the porch was before them: and the other pillars and the thick beam were before them. Then he made a porch for the throne where he might judge, even the porch of judgment: and it was covered with cedar from one side of the floor to the other. And his house where he dwelt had another court within the porch, which was of the like work. Solomon made also an house for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he had taken to wife, like unto this porch.

schools.summary: Delitzsch infers the pillar-hall's position from its place in the list, makes the throne-hall and judgment-hall one room marked off only by the repeated verb, calls the phrase about the cedar covering very obscure and refuses the rendering that makes it panelling, and puts the royal quarters behind the throne-hall with a court of their own; Ellicott reads the pillared porch as an entrance vestibule to the hall of state on the strength of the matching dimensions, treats the judgment hall as a separate building, and reports Fergusson's square four-pillared reconstruction from Assyrian and Persian remains.

Gill places the pillared porch at the west end of the house, recalls the ivory throne on which the king sat to hear causes, and identifies the dwelling as the part of the complex where Solomon actually resided.

Clarke notes that one porch was given over to judgment, which Solomon administered in person, and counts three houses that probably formed a single building distinguished by use — palace, court-house, and the apartments for the women.

debates.question: Was the hall of judgment a separate building or the same room as the throne hall?

positions.position: One and the same hall, serving as court and audience chamber, immediately beyond the pillared hall.
Plainly a separate building, undescribed in the text except as floored and ceiled with cedar.

themes: And he made a porch of pillars; the length thereof was fifty cubits, and the breadth thereof thirty cubits: and the porch was before them: and the other pillars and the thick beam were before them.
Then he made a porch for the throne where he might judge, even the porch of judgment: and it was covered with cedar from one side of the floor to the other.
And his house where he dwelt had another court within the porch, which was of the like work. Solomon made also an house for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he had taken to wife, like unto this porch.

9.pericope_label: All these were of costly stones, according to the measures of hewed stones, sawed with saws, within and without, even from the foundation unto the coping, and so on the outside toward the great court. And the foundation was of costly stones, even great stones, stones of ten cubits, and stones of eight cubits. And above were costly stones, after the measures of hewed stones, and cedars. And the great court round about was with three rows of hewed stones, and a row of cedar beams, both for the inner court of the house of the Lord, and for the porch of the house.

schools.summary: Delitzsch extends the clause to every building described, has the stones sawn on the inner and outer face alike, renders the upper limit as the corbels carrying the roof beams and refuses the reading that makes it a roof parapet, and defends the comparison of the great court with the temple's inner court on grammatical grounds; Ellicott accepts that resemblance and infers an enclosure taking in the whole palace, with inner courts besides.

Gill names the costly stones as marble, porphyry and the like, takes the foundation blocks to be of great price as well as great size, traces the same masonry from the foundation to the ceiling, and says only of the great court that it surrounded Solomon's house.

themes: All these were of costly stones, according to the measures of hewed stones, sawed with saws, within and without, even from the foundation unto the coping, and so on the outside toward the great court.
And the foundation was of costly stones, even great stones, stones of ten cubits, and stones of eight cubits.
And above were costly stones, after the measures of hewed stones, and cedars.
And the great court round about was with three rows of hewed stones, and a row of cedar beams, both for the inner court of the house of the Lord, and for the porch of the house.

13.pericope_label: And king Solomon sent and fetched Hiram out of Tyre. He was a widow’s son of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in brass: and he was filled with wisdom, and understanding, and cunning to work all works in brass. And he came to king Solomon, and wrought all his work.

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the verb as a pluperfect and the verse as a supplementary remark, explains the epithet in the parallel as a title of honour rather than a family claim, harmonises the parentage as a Danite married into Naphtali, and ends with the text's own verdict on the man's skill; Ellicott turns to the Chronicler's fuller account, where Solomon asks for a man cunning to work.

Gill separates the craftsman from the king of Tyre, passes on the name Hyperon from Clemens of Alexandria, and lays out three ways of reconciling the tribal notices, adding that any error belongs to the king of Tyre whose words the Chronicler reports rather than to the sacred historian.

Clarke calls him an intelligent coppersmith of Jewish extraction on his mother's side, allows that the king of Tyre may simply have confounded the two tribes, and admits the versions and manuscripts give no help.

Henry makes the mixed descent the point — the head of a Tyrian and the heart of an Israelite — and sets it in a longer line, that as the tabernacle was built with the wealth of Egypt so the temple was built with the wit of Tyre, God serving himself by the common gifts of men.

debates.question: How can the mother be of Naphtali here and of the daughters of Dan in the parallel?

positions.position: She was a Danite by birth who married into Naphtali.
Several reconciliations are open — the city of Dan lay in Naphtali, or her mother was the Danite, or she was of Dan and her husband of Naphtali.
Either she was Naphtali by her father and Dan by her mother, or the king of Tyre confused the tribes; the evidence does not decide.

themes: And king Solomon sent and fetched Hiram out of Tyre.

He was a widow’s son of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in brass: and he was filled with wisdom, and understanding, and cunning to work all works in brass. And he came to king Solomon, and wrought all his work.

15.pericope_label: For he cast two pillars of brass, of eighteen cubits high apiece: and a line of twelve cubits did compass either of them about. And he made two chapiters of molten brass, to set upon the tops of the pillars: the height of the one chapiter was five cubits, and the height of the other chapiter was five cubits: And nets of checker work, and wreaths of chain work, for the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars; seven for the one chapiter, and seven for the other chapiter. And he made the pillars, and two rows round about upon the one network, to cover the chapiters that were upon the top, with pomegranates: and so did he for the other chapiter.

schools.summary: Delitzsch sets the capitals at five cubits and traces the shorter figure elsewhere to a copyist's confusion of two letters, counts seven plaited festoons to each capital, and repairs the exchanged words for pillars and pomegranates before placing a row of pomegranates above and below the plaiting; Ellicott judges the number seven itself corrupt and would read a net-work for each capital.

Gill reconciles the eighteen cubits here with the thirty-five given for the pair either by rounding or by allowing half a cubit in each to the pedestal or capital, so that the text measures only what was visible; he pictures the capitals as crowns or joined crowns, and reads the checker work as boughs and leaves and the chain work as fringes.
Clarke converts the height to about thirty feet, gives the circumference at twelve cubits, and doubts a founder could be found even now to cast masses of that size.

outliers.claim: That the reading giving seven plaits to each capital is erroneous, and the clause should speak simply of a net-work for the one capital and a net-work for the other.

themes: For he cast two pillars of brass, of eighteen cubits high apiece: and a line of twelve cubits did compass either of them about.
And he made two chapiters of molten brass, to set upon the tops of the pillars: the height of the one chapiter was five cubits, and the height of the other chapiter was five cubits:
And nets of checker work, and wreaths of chain work, for the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars; seven for the one chapiter, and seven for the other chapiter.
And he made the pillars, and two rows round about upon the one network, to cover the chapiters that were upon the top, with pomegranates: and so did he for the other chapiter.

19.pericope_label: And the chapiters that were upon the top of the pillars were of lily work in the porch, four cubits. And the chapiters upon the two pillars had pomegranates also above, over against the belly which was by the network: and the pomegranates were two hundred in rows round about upon the other chapiter. And he set up the pillars in the porch of the temple: and he set up the right pillar, and called the name thereof Jachin: and he set up the left pillar, and called the name thereof Boaz. And upon the top of the pillars was lily work: so was the work of the pillars finished.

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes the lily work as a crown on the upper part of the capital, proving the plaiting covered only the lower, calls the four-cubit clause obscure, and settles the pillars' position from the parallel's before the house, so that they stood free in front of the hall and bore no roof; Ellicott renders over against as close to, explains the belly as the capital's swell where it meets the shaft, and supplies an omitted clause to reach the total of four hundred pomegranates.

Gill reads the lily work as the open lily flower, fixes the pillars at the entrance into the porch rather than into the temple against Jarchi, and follows Lightfoot in reading the sense of the pomegranate band without the supplied words.
Clarke gives the two names as he shall establish and in strength, and calls the pillars emblematical since they seem to have supported no part of the building.

Henry doubts they were memorials of the pillar of cloud and fire and takes them for memoranda to priests and worshippers not to lean on their own sufficiency — the one name answering the wandering heart, the other the weakness that cannot perform — and reads in them a promise that the worship established there would stand, noting that the record of the temple's destruction takes particular notice of the breaking of these pillars.

debates.question: Did the pillars stand free before the hall or inside it, carrying the roof?

positions.position: Free in front of the hall, on its right and left, as the parallel twice says; the arguments for the other view have no force.
Whatever their position, they supported no part of the building and were purely emblematic.

themes: And the chapiters that were upon the top of the pillars were of lily work in the porch, four cubits.
And the chapiters upon the two pillars had pomegranates also above, over against the belly which was by the network: and the pomegranates were two hundred in rows round about upon the other chapiter.
And he set up the pillars in the porch of the temple: and he set up the right pillar, and called the name thereof Jachin: and he set up the left pillar, and called the name thereof Boaz.
And upon the top of the pillars was lily work: so was the work of the pillars finished.

23.pericope_label: And he made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other: it was round all about, and his height was five cubits: and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about. And under the brim of it round about there were knops compassing it, ten in a cubit, compassing the sea round about: the knops were cast in two rows, when it was cast. It stood upon twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east: and the sea was set above upon them, and all their hinder parts were inward. And it was an hand breadth thick, and the brim thereof was wrought like the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies: it contained two thousand baths.

schools.summary: Delitzsch names the basin for its size, gives diameter, height and circumference and observes how near the round numbers come to the true ratio, refuses the harmonisation of gourds with oxen since the parallel's word means oxen and not their heads, sets the twelve oxen three to each quarter on a metal plate, and prefers two thousand baths to three since the dimensions cannot hold more.

Gill explains the name from Jewish usage for any large collection of waters, reports the ornaments as oval so that the Targum calls them figures of eggs, allows that they may be gourds bearing oxen heads and serving as taps, and gives the metal's thickness as four fingers.

Henry notices that the basin stood so high the priests needed either steps or taps, recalls that the drawers of water for the house of God kept it filled, passes on the suggestion that the oxen were cast in contempt of the calf, and reads the enlargement from the tabernacle's laver to the temple's sea as a sign of fuller provision for cleansing under the gospel.

debates.question: Are the ornaments under the brim gourds or figures of oxen?

positions.position: They may be reconciled: gourd-shaped, bearing the heads of oxen, perhaps serving as taps.
They cannot; the parallel reading is an error of the pen, since its word means oxen and not the heads of oxen.

outliers.claim: That the twelve oxen may have been cast in contempt of the golden calf, so the people might see such figures were fitter to make posts of than gods of — an expedient the event showed to avail very little.

themes: And he made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other: it was round all about, and his height was five cubits: and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about.
And under the brim of it round about there were knops compassing it, ten in a cubit, compassing the sea round about: the knops were cast in two rows, when it was cast.

It stood upon twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east: and the sea was set above upon them, and all their hinder parts were inward.
And it was an hand breadth thick, and the brim thereof was wrought like the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies: it contained two thousand baths.

27.pericope_label: And he made ten bases of brass; four cubits was the length of one base, and four cubits the breadth thereof, and three cubits the height of it. And the work of the bases was on this manner: they had borders, and the borders were between the ledges: And on the borders that were between the ledges were lions, oxen, and cherubims: and upon the ledges there was a base above: and beneath the lions and oxen were certain additions made of thin work. And every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass: and the four corners thereof had undersetters: under the laver were undersetters molten, at the side of every addition.

schools.summary: Delitzsch derives the name from the office of supporting the basins in which the sacrificial flesh was washed, gives the chests as four cubits square and three high with panelled sides framed and joined at the angles, rejects the report of three compartments a side as leaving the figures absurdly small, and takes the wheels for ordinary carriage wheels with the chest raised on feet above their rims so the stands could be moved.

Gill calls the stands seats or settles for the lavers, treats the panel figures as ornament and infers that the cherubim, being distinguished from lions and oxen, were figures of men or of eagles, and denies that the wheels were for carriage — they were set one at each corner rather than paired like a chariot's, and once the lavers were placed the stands were fixed.
Clarke calls them pedestals for the ten lavers to rest on.
Henry reads the wheels as provision for removing the lavers as occasion required.

debates.question: Were the wheeled stands built to be moved?

positions.position: Yes — wheels after the style of a carriage, with the chest lifted clear on feet so the stands could be driven from place to place.
No — the wheels were supports resting on brass plates, set one at each corner rather than paired, and the stands were fixed once the lavers were on them.

themes: And he made ten bases of brass; four cubits was the length of one base, and four cubits the breadth thereof, and three cubits the height of it.
And the work of the bases was on this manner: they had borders, and the borders were between the ledges:
And on the borders that were between the ledges were lions, oxen, and cherubims: and upon the ledges there was a base above: and beneath the lions and oxen were certain additions made of thin work.
And every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass: and the four corners thereof had undersetters: under the laver were undersetters molten, at the side of every addition.

31.pericope_label: And the mouth of it within the chapiter and above was a cubit: but the mouth thereof was round after the work of the base, a cubit and an half: and also upon the mouth of it were gravings with their borders, foursquare, not round. And under the borders were four wheels; and the axletrees of the wheels were joined to the base: and the height of a wheel was a cubit and half a cubit. And the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten. And there were four undersetters to the four corners of one base: and the undersetters were of the very base itself. And in the top of the base was there a round compass of half a cubit high: and on the top of the base the ledges thereof and the borders thereof were of the same.

schools.summary: Delitzsch builds the same shape from a dome-like covering with a pillar-capital rising at its centre to receive the basin's lower rim, and below gives four wheels a cubit and a half high with axles, naves, felloes and spokes all cast rather than assembled, the arched lid standing half a cubit above the sides with its holders and panels cast out of the same piece; Ellicott calls the passage most obscure, rejects that reconstruction as arbitrary for rendering one word first of the laver and then of the crown, and proposes instead that the circular stand caught the drippings, the engraved panels being the corner spaces left by a round stand on a square top.

Gill describes a smaller circular base rising from the lid like a coronet, hollow so the laver's foot could sit into it, going up straight half a cubit and widening half a cubit more; he matches the wheel to a chariot wheel in form, calls the corner supports pillars, and identifies the round compass with the coronet already described.

debates.question: Whose mouth does the verse describe?

positions.position: The laver within the crown, then the crown itself — a rendering that makes the upper stand a pedestal for the basin.
Neither confidently; to render the same word now of the laver and now of the crown is arbitrary, and the passage stays obscure.

outliers.claim: That the circular stand may have been there to catch the drippings if the basin was emptied by a tap near its bottom, and that the engraved panels are the corner spaces left where a round stand sits on a square top.

themes: And the mouth of it within the chapiter and above was a cubit: but the mouth thereof was round after the work of the base, a cubit and an half: and also upon the mouth of it were gravings with their borders, foursquare, not round.
And under the borders were four wheels; and the axletrees of the wheels were joined to the base: and the height of a wheel was a cubit and half a cubit.
And the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten.
And there were four undersetters to the four corners of one base: and the undersetters were of the very base itself.
And in the top of the base was there a round compass of half a cubit high: and on the top of the base the ledges thereof and the borders thereof were of the same.

36.pericope_label: For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about. After this manner he made the ten bases: all of them had one casting, one measure, and one size. Then made he ten lavers of brass: one laver contained forty baths: and every laver was four cubits: and upon every one of the ten bases one laver. And he put five bases on the right side of the house, and five on the left side of the house: and he set the sea on the right side of the house eastward over against the south.

schools.summary: Delitzsch lists the engraving as cherubim, lions and palm trees with wreaths, reads the summary as insisting on one casting, measure and form for all ten, argues the four cubits must be the basins' width since they sat on top of the stands, infers a wide-spreading shell shape from the crown of only a cubit and a half, and fixes right as south and left as north, ranging the stands along the sides of the hall with the sea forward between hall and altar; Ellicott places the sea at the south-eastern corner with the lavers five to a side.

Gill notes that the word rendered ledges here differs from the earlier one, reports the Targum's axle trees and the literal sense of hands, and passes on the tradition from Procopius Gazaeus of hands holding a circle like a crown; he recalls the tabernacle's single laver, takes the ten as a figure of the provision in the blood of Christ, and hesitates over which side is the right, since a man entering from the east has the north on his right hand.
Clarke divides the uses exactly: the lavers held water for washing the victims, the sea was where the priests washed themselves, and the whole was a work of vast art, labour and expense.

Henry gives each laver's capacity as about ten barrels, says the ten ordinarily stood in two rows of five, and draws the lesson that those must be very clean who bear the vessels of the Lord, the washing being often because the defilement is daily.

debates.question: Which side of the house is the right?

positions.position: The south, with the left the north.
Commonly the south, but the eastward entrance makes a man walking in have the north on his right.

themes: For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about.
After this manner he made the ten bases: all of them had one casting, one measure, and one size.
Then made he ten lavers of brass: one laver contained forty baths: and every laver was four cubits: and upon every one of the ten bases one laver.
And he put five bases on the right side of the house, and five on the left side of the house: and he set the sea on the right side of the house eastward over against the south.

40.pericope_label: And Hiram made the lavers, and the shovels, and the basons. So Hiram made an end of doing all the work that he made king Solomon for the house of the Lord: The two pillars, and the two bowls of the chapiters that were on the top of the two pillars; and the two networks, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars; And four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, even two rows of pomegranates for one network, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters that were upon the pillars; And the ten bases, and ten lavers on the bases; And one sea, and twelve oxen under the sea;

schools.summary: Delitzsch sets out the section's order — court brass, then a second run through the pillars, stands, sea and lesser vessels, then the gold — observes that the list runs almost word for word with the Chronicler's except for the altar, lampstands, table and great court, corrects the phrase putting the capitals on the pillars' surface, and rejects as apocryphal the Greek addition counting forty-eight pillars for both houses; Ellicott would read pots for lavers and concludes the altar's absence is simply a gap in the record, since the Chronicler and Josephus both say Hiram made one and give its size.

Gill follows Jarchi and Ben Gersom in identifying these lavers with the pots for carrying off the altar's ashes, explains the shovels as a kind of besom and the basins as vessels for catching and sprinkling the blood, and notices that both the brazen altar and the fleshhooks go unmentioned.

Clarke is astonished by the speed, that one artist with however many assistants could design and execute works of this magnitude, taste and variety in so short a time, against which the building of the house itself was a small matter.
Henry reads the abundance of utensils as foresight rather than excess, a stock laid in against the wearing out of the first, Solomon providing for those who would come after.

themes: And Hiram made the lavers, and the shovels, and the basons. So Hiram made an end of doing all the work that he made king Solomon for the house of the Lord:
The two pillars, and the two bowls of the chapiters that were on the top of the two pillars; and the two networks, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars;
And four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, even two rows of pomegranates for one network, to cover the two bowls of the chapiters that were upon the pillars;
And the ten bases, and ten lavers on the bases;
And one sea, and twelve oxen under the sea;

46.pericope_label: In the plain of Jordan did the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan. And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because they were exceeding many: neither was the weight of the brass found out.

schools.summary: Delitzsch places Succoth beyond the Jordan on the south side of the Jabbok and Zarthan on the near side at Kurn Sartabeh, argues the casting-place must have been western since the eastern bank has almost no level ground, cites a traveller for the marly soil, refuses the reading that makes the king lay the vessels down rather than let them lie unweighed, and traces the brass to Hadadezer's cities and Toi's gift; Ellicott names the same places with their territories and wonders how those cities came to be so rich in brass, pointing to the ancient copper workings of the Sinai peninsula.

Gill explains that the thick close clay took moulds into which the melted brass was poured, and that although the text credits the king the work was Hiram's at his orders; on the weighing he says the vessels were laid up in the sanctuary unweighed because so many and so large, following the Targum's sense of the verb.
Clarke agrees the particular clay drew them there and reports that opinion is divided over which bank held the foundry, one writer placing it near Bethshan.

Henry adds that Solomon would not have such dirty, smoky work carried on near Jerusalem, and finds the missing tally creditable on both sides — workmen honest enough to need no account, and brass plentiful enough that none was feared short.

positions.position: In the plain of Jordan, between Succoth and Zarthan, on the western bank.
In the plain of Jericho, in the clay ground.

themes: In the plain of Jordan did the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan.
And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because they were exceeding many: neither was the weight of the brass found out.

48.pericope_label: And Solomon made all the vessels that pertained unto the house of the Lord: the altar of gold, and the table of gold, whereupon the shewbread was, And the candlesticks of pure gold, five on the right side, and five on the left, before the oracle, with the flowers, and the lamps, and the tongs of gold, And the bowls, and the snuffers, and the basons, and the spoons, and the censers of pure gold; and the hinges of gold, both for the doors of the inner house, the most holy place, and for the doors of the house, to wit, of the temple.

schools.summary: Delitzsch sorts the vessels into two classes of costly gold and a third of gold less pure, warns against narrowing the house of the Lord to the Holy Place alone, and takes the golden door fittings for the sockets in which the door pegs turned; Ellicott identifies the golden altar as the altar of incense and shows that the incense presupposed a sacrifice already offered, reads the shewbread as bread of the presence returned to God out of his own gift, prefers that the ten lampstands stood beside the old sevenfold one rather than replacing it, and corrects the renderings of snuffers, spoons and censers.

Gill says all that had stood in the tabernacle was made again except the ark, mercy seat and cherubim, sets the ten lampstands in the Holy Place before the oracle, reports the Jewish tradition ranging them beside the old lampstand of Moses rather than the room, takes the multiplication as a figure of the greater light under the gospel, and notes that the bowls were for the oil.

Henry observes that the gold work was done last and the work of the house ended with it, that the altar of incense remained one as Christ and his intercession are one, and that the ten tables and lampstands intimate greater plenty of spiritual food and heavenly light than the law afforded — even the door hinges being gold so that everything should be alike magnificent.

debates.question: Did the ten lampstands replace the sevenfold lampstand of the tabernacle?

positions.position: More probably they stood beside it, since the old vessel is unlikely to have been disused and the second temple had only the one.
The ten stood on either side of the lampstand of Moses, which remained in place.

outliers.claim: That the splendour may have been meant to keep the people from idolatry, no idol-temple being so rich — an expedient whose failure the event showed.

themes: And Solomon made all the vessels that pertained unto the house of the Lord: the altar of gold, and the table of gold, whereupon the shewbread was,
And the candlesticks of pure gold, five on the right side, and five on the left, before the oracle, with the flowers, and the lamps, and the tongs of gold,

And the bowls, and the snuffers, and the basons, and the spoons, and the censers of pure gold; and the hinges of gold, both for the doors of the inner house, the most holy place, and for the doors of the house, to wit, of the temple.

51.pericope_label: So was ended all the work that king Solomon made for the house of the Lord. And Solomon brought in the things which David his father had dedicated; even the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, did he put among the treasures of the house of the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the accumulation enormous and evidently the work of years out of the spoils of many victories, quotes David's own acknowledgement that riches and honour come from God and that what was given had first been received, and reads the wording as indicating that bullion in money or ingots came in besides the finished vessels.
Gill reads the closing clause as covering everything Solomon ordered made for the house, whether for ornament or for use and service, and notes the whole was finished within seven years.

Clarke takes the verse to answer whether any of David's provision was spent on the building — apparently none, since the dedicated things come in only after the house stands finished — infers four years of preparation before the work began and a continuing appropriation of public revenue during it, and concludes the temple was truly Solomon's, who found the materials and bore every expense.

Henry says what the building had not consumed was laid up against repairs, emergencies and the standing charge of the service, and turns it on the reader: what parents have dedicated to God the children ought not to take back or divert, but to devote cheerfully to its intended uses.

outliers.claim: That the temple was truly Solomon's rather than David's, since Solomon provided all its materials and bore every expense, his father's dedicated treasure being stored untouched.
